articles.snippet: Vinicius wants protection for players like him, Yamal and Alvarez 'who bring something different to the game.'
articles.full_text:
Real Madrid’s Vinicius says he’s being targeted by referees
Vinicius wants protection for players like himself, Yamal and Alvarez ‘who bring something different to the game.’
Vinicius Junior is not happy with how he is being treated by referees and wants more protection for talented players like him, Lamine Yamal and Julian Alvarez.
The Brazil forward spoke out after Real Madrid’s 4-3 come-from-behind win at Roma in the Champions League on Wednesday.
He acknowledged that he is going through a slump, but said he had “no doubt” he will regain his best form soon.
The match against Roma came hours after he was handed a four-game suspension in the Spanish league after being sent off for pulling the hair of an opponent and for protesting against the referee.
“I don’t recall any other player receiving a four-match suspension. I tried to move the player in front of me out of the way and I ended up getting caught in his hair,” Vinicius said.
“That was it – a red card – which is why I was so surprised. I didn’t say a single offensive word to the referee that would warrant a four-match ban. But when it comes to Vini, it’s all too easy.
“The opposing team will always say it’s justified and the press will say the same. I understand that. I’m here to keep evolving and improving, because I know where I’ve come from and what I’m capable of achieving,” Vinicius added.
“It’s understandable for the opposing fans to jeer me, because my job is to score goals against their team, but I don’t get the referees.
“I’ve seen the stats: I’ve been on the receiving end of 500 fouls, yet that has only resulted in five red cards. In the end, the yellow cards always seem to go to Vini, to the attacking players. We need to protect the players who bring something different to the game, like Lamine at Barcelona or Julian at Atleti. Defenders are allowed to foul me the entire match but in the end it’s me who gets the card.”
Madrid coach Jose Mourinho complained about the timing of the announcement of the suspension.
“Do you think it’s normal for a player from a Spanish team, preparing for an important match that’s also crucial for Spanish football, to find out about his four-match suspension just two hours before kickoff?” Mourinho said.
“We were on the bus about to arrive at the stadium when we found out … they’ve started doing things without any shame.”
Vinicius, who hasn’t scored for Madrid since August, was replaced in the 59th minute of Madrid’s victory before the team rallied from 3-1 down.
“I’m working to get back to my best as soon as possible,” Vinicius said. “I know I’m not at my peak right now, but I’ve been through worse and even when people have doubted me, I’ve always stood up for this club. That’s why I signed a six-year contract extension.
“The good run of form will return and the goals will come back, too. I’m certain of that. I have no doubt. I’m here to help the team.”
The 26-year-old Vinicius has scored only two goals for club and country this season, one for Madrid in the team’s second league match and another with Brazil in a friendly against Australia in September.
He downplayed his frustration after Mourinho substituted him on Wednesday.
“It’s natural for me to get upset when I’m substituted because I always want to play every single match. I’m well aware of my current form and how I’m playing. I’m here to help the team and sometimes you have to come off so that other players can get on and change the dynamic,” he said.
“Mourinho and I have a great relationship. He’s always straight with me. Of course I got a little annoyed when I came off today, but that’s normal. In the end he was right, the team improved and that’s what matters most.”
Vinícius was replaced by Endrick, who scored an 85th-minute equaliser before Antonio Rudiger gave Madrid the win in the 90th.
“This is Real Madrid. We needed a match like this to shift the dynamic and turn the season around a bit,” Vinicius said. “It’s going to help and give us a boost because the younger players stepped up. They played a great game.
“Endrick played an incredible match. He scored and really helped us out. That’s why he was named man of the match.”
Because of his suspension, Vinicius will miss Sunday’s home match against Sevilla and the following week’s trip for “el Clasico” against Barcelona. He will also miss away matches at Racing Santander and Valencia.

articles.title: Pentagon seeks expertise to develop brain injury assessment standards
articles.snippet: The Defense Department is seeking a variety of information that can help in formulating standards for assessing mild traumatic brain injuries, or mTBI.
articles.full_text:
The Pentagon is looking to create standards to assess the impact of blast-induced mild traumatic brain injuries.
The goal is to have benchmarks that will allow assessment of the “physiological and biomechanical effects of blast injuries” caused by explosions of enemy munitions or the blast effects from firing friendly weapons, according to the Request for Information by the Blast Injury Research Coordinating Office, or BIRCO, within U.S. Army Medical Research and Development Command.
This will enable “risk assessment of military service members who are exposed to blunt impacts resulting from acceleration of the body, blunt injury from a ballistic strike to the helmet, or effects from blast pressure produced by a weapon system or explosion,” the RFI reads.
BIRCO is seeking a variety of information that can help formulate standards for assessing mild traumatic brain injuries, or mTBI. The information could include existing criteria, standards and models for brain injuries, as well as identifying experts on the topic.
The Pentagon is also seeking input from manufacturers of protective gear that can be “highly relevant to understanding human tolerance limits and predicting blast injuries.”
The RFI uses a broad definition of blast injuries, including the effects on the body of blast-wave overpressure, fragments, the human body being thrown against hard objects, collapsing buildings and burns, as well as the effects of toxic gases and radiation.
“The standards can range from simple dose response curves and injury thresholds that address single components of blast insults, such as blast pressure wave magnitude, or address multiple components of blast insults, such as pressure magnitude over time,” the RFI said.
These standards will be used for “health hazard assessments, survivability assessments, and protection system development aimed at producing safe weapon systems, survivable combat platforms, and effective protection systems.”
The effects of traumatic brain injuries on military personnel have become better known in recent years. There is evidence that exposure to the blast of firing artillery, tank guns and handheld missiles, as well as being thrown around while riding small boats used by special operations forces, leads to brain trauma, or even TBI.
Department of Defense data from the Iran war shows a relatively high proportion of head trauma from Iranian missile and drone strikes.
The RFI was published after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide baseline cognitive assessments to troops. Across the services, the Defense Department is hampered by staff shortages and a lack of technology needed to conduct the assessments, the GAO found.
The Pentagon announced in April that it will begin a one-year pilot program to test a new cognitive assessment tool, an app that service members can use to complete assessments. DoD officials said the app will be less resource-intensive than current assessments and will help improve the services’ ability to track exposures.
Veterans who have suffered traumatic brain injuries are more than twice as likely to die by suicide, according to a 2019 study.
Michael Peck is a correspondent for Defense News and a columnist for the Center for European Policy Analysis. He holds an M.A. in political science from Rutgers University. Find him at theuncommondefense.com. His email is mikedefense1@gmail.com.

articles.title: US ‘economic supremacy’ key in the Western Hemisphere, top US Army general says
articles.snippet: The U.S. Army’s top commander for the Western Hemisphere described American “economic supremacy” as an overarching national security goal.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Army’s top commander for the Western Hemisphere described American “economic supremacy” as an overarching goal of Washington’s regional security strategy, outlining plans to expand its military footprint in Central and South America on Monday at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting.
The 2025 National Security Strategy prioritizes economic dominance in the Western Hemisphere through national security, Gen. Joseph Ryan, the commander of the U.S. Army Western Hemisphere Command, said during a panel discussion with Gen. Luis Cardozo, Colombian attaché, and Vice Adm. Jo-Ann Burdian, the U.S. Coast Guard’s Atlantic Area Commander.
“The end state is economic supremacy for the United States,” Ryan said, later adding, “We have ceded control of that economic terrain in this hemisphere to the People’s Republic of China over at least the last two decades, and that is a major threat to our national security.”
Ryan pointed to Panama as an example, explaining how a high percentage of trade to and from the United States passes through the Panama Canal. He said the Panamanian government saw a mutual benefit in the partnership. It also allows the U.S. to “keep an eye on those states that are aligned with other adversaries in the region,” he said, such as Cuba, Nicaragua and formerly Venezuela. Lebanese Hezbollah has a presence in the area, he added.
Recently, the U.S. military co-led PANAMAX, a massive multinational exercise hosted in Panama for the first time since 2012, where forces practiced defending the Panama Canal. During the exercise, which included personnel from 19 countries, including Argentina, Brazil, Peru, Chile and Colombia, troops drilled command post and field exercises.
Countering cartels
In addition to countering China, the Defense Department has railed against cartels, prioritizing counter-cartel operations in the Western Hemisphere.
Burdian said the cartels are trafficking people, narcotics and bulk cash. She characterized them as “multi-billion-dollar organizations that operate globally and are unconstrained in the ways we are — they are unconstrained financially,” she said, adding, “and they demonstrate extraordinary agility, and they certainly are unfettered by rules or basic human decency.”
Cardozo said his country — Colombia — has seen how cartels can build diverse, enormous economies.
“In Colombia, it’s not only using the drug trafficking as a main source of income, they also use illegal mining,” he said, which can destroy the environment and people’s homes, but reap huge financial rewards. “I think that’s their Achilles’ heel: the illegal financing. If we take that money away from them, they’re going to asphyxiate.”
With the Army’s logistics assistance, Burdian said the Coast Guard is working to establish an Expeditionary Cutter Squadron with two ships in Panama to conduct interdiction operations. Ryan said officials recently approved a capacity increase for Joint Task Force Bravo — a forward-deployed task force based at Soto Cano Air Base in Comayagua, Honduras — to expand the footprint over the next few fiscal years.
Ryan said the task force would receive more rotary-wing aircraft and personnel to “address some of the natural disasters and threats in the region.” Those additional resources, he said, “become absolutely critical when you’re talking about moving supplies, moving people to the point of need, and making assessments.”
Command restructure
In a major force restructure, the Army stood up the Western Hemisphere Command in December 2025, combining U.S. Army North, U.S. Army South and Armed Forces Command under a single headquarters. As its focus shifted, the Army revived its jungle school in Panama’s “Green Hell” and approved service-wide wear of the Jungle tab.
In August, U.S. Southern Command activated Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere, a new headquarters to unify operations with allies and partners, including the 18 partner nations of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition. The new task force replaced Operation Southern Spear, which has destroyed scores of sea vessels as part of what the Trump administration characterizes as a counternarcotics campaign. More than 210 people have been killed in the attacks.
The strikes have drawn controversy, and the Trump administration has offered little evidence of drug-trafficking activity. The Defense Department’s inspector general launched an investigation into whether U.S. Southern Command followed protocols with the strikes, but the White House has emphatically defended the attacks.
Ryan said that joint exercises with partner forces in the region will increasingly center on counter-cartel operations.
“We are going to focus our exercise programming going forward to be really focused on those things that contribute to the counter-designated terrorist organization threat and cartel threat in the region,” he told the crowd.
Publicly available technology is fueling the cartel’s economy, the panelists emphasized.
“Make no mistake, you know, Starlink is great as long as you’re using it on your side. When it pervades to the adversary side, it becomes very difficult to counter,” Ryan said, emphasizing that the military cannot stop cartels from accessing publicly available technology.
Ryan said the intelligence is showing an increase in unmanned aerial systems for human trafficking operations, and Burdian said the Coast Guard is used to seeing homemade submersibles from the cartels coming out of riverine terrain off the coast of Colombia. But now, as the markets grow, they are seeing them move across the Atlantic.
“The greatest threat I face — the most persistent threat, frankly — is the commingling of illicit traffic or threats or another nature with legitimate traffic,” Burdian said.
Only completely closing a port can eliminate all illegal traffic, she said, but that is economically destructive.
“So, how do you know what to let in? How do you know what to keep out?” she asked. “How do I enable those commanders on scene to allow the legitimate commerce to pass in and out while at the same time, identifying and neutralizing threats before they damage the U.S. economy or kill Americans?”
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Thales Australia tackles heavy battlefield logistics with new big-rig robot
articles.snippet: Thales Australia is working on autonomy features for its new big-rig cargo robot that can carry a 20-foot container or act as a large battery in the field.
articles.full_text:
PERTH, Australia — Imagine an unmanned ground vehicle large enough to cart a 20-foot container around the battlefield, as well as possessing sufficient power to run a radar or launch a barrage of missiles.
Thales Australia says it has built just such a robot.
The company unveiled its BladeHaul extra-large, heavy-duty UGV on Oct. 6, the opening day of the Land Forces 2026 exhibition being held in Perth, Western Australia.
Looking something akin to an aircraft tug, the BladeHaul relies on the chassis and driveline of Thales Australia’s popular Bushmaster 4x4 protected mobility vehicle that is in widespread Australian Army use.
According to its designer, this uncrewed vehicle “is engineered to outperform all existing and planned counterparts in payload capacity and operational flexibility.”
Official specs list a payload capacity of 10-plus tons for this cargo UGV, and a driving range comparable to that of the Bushmaster’s 600-plus kilometers.
The Bushmaster’s original mechanicals have been replaced by a hybrid energy and battery storage solution from 3ME Technology, Thales Australia’s partner in the effort.
3ME Technology has extensive experience in the mining sector, and it previously developed a hybrid-engined Bushmaster vehicle.
For the BladeHaul the company has assembled a 660V power system that offers 110kWh of power.
Justin Bain, CEO of 3ME Technology, said: “Working with Thales Australia brings together the best of Australian innovation, combining 3ME Technology’s systems engineering and platform development capabilities with the Bushmaster’s proven performance and established manufacturing base. Together we’re delivering an entirely new XL-UGV at a time when demand for contested logistics and remote power solutions for littoral environments is present and growing.”
Thales Australia envisages three potential use cases for the BladeHaul: as a cargo mover in zones of contested logistics; as a mobile and enduring power source for other equipment; and as a highly mobile platform for sensors and effectors.
The vehicle could therefore find utility in tasks such as carrying coastal anti-ship missiles, as a counter-drone system, mounting an air surveillance radar, reloading munitions or detecting mines. For the latter mission, it could have a mine plow or rollers mounted on the front.
The manufacturer says the vehicle’s applications are limited only by the imagination of the user. For example, it could carry containerized missile systems or launch drone swarms, one official told Defense News.
Alternatively, it could generate and supply power for a field hospital, a command post or simply act as a standalone generator. It offers a 1MW of power. To put that in perspective, 1MW could simultaneously power 1,000 homes.
To add to its versatility, the BladeHaul 4x4 UGV can fit in transport aircraft like the C-130 and A400M.
The BladeHaul is not yet ready for action, however. Work on the project began 18 months ago, with progress really accelerating over the past six months, but it does not yet have a working autonomy system.
Thales Australia signed a memorandum of understanding with Deakin University at Land Forces 2026 to develop its autonomy suite. This will build upon the suite used on the smaller Guardian Angel UGV unveiled by Thales earlier this year. It will be capable of remote, fully autonomous or follow-me operations, for example.
Thales Australia said in a statement: “By integrating advanced autonomy that enables human-machine teaming, hybrid technology, heavy payload capacity and power generation within a single platform, Thales Australia and 3ME Technology are delivering a next-generation solution that enhances operational readiness and supports Australia’s commitment to sovereign defense innovation.”
The BladeHaul is aimed at the Australian Army, but its appeal extends to any land force, according to the manufacturer.
The vehicle has no V-shaped hull to protect against underbody blasts, as there is no crew aboard. However, ballistic protection could be added to it depending on the function.
Bain said there is interest in a UGV version able to carry a 40-foot container too. “If there’s sufficient demand, we may look at that.”
Gordon Arthur is an Asia correspondent for Defense News. After a 20-year stint working in Hong Kong, he now resides in New Zealand. He has attended military exercises and defense exhibitions in about 20 countries around the Asia-Pacific region.

articles.title: ‘Who doesn’t want to be first?’ Best Squad, NCO and Soldier named at AUSA
articles.snippet: The five-soldier squad from the 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment was named the Best Squad during a ceremony at AUSA on Monday.
articles.full_text:
After a multi-day gauntlet of obstacle courses, ruck marches and technical trials that tested human endurance and proficiency, the five-soldier squad from the 3rd Battalion, 75th Ranger Regiment was named the Best Squad during a ceremony at the Association of the U.S. Army Annual Meeting and Exposition on Monday.
From Sept. 11 to 19, 11 squads battled at Fort Benning, Georgia, to earn the titles of Soldier of the Year, Noncommissioned Officer of the Year and Best Squad.
Cpl. Michael Shield was named the Army’s Soldier of the Year, and Staff Sgt. Colin Doyle as the Army’s non-commissioned officer of the year. The announcement cements the Rangers as a dominant force within the Army competition, with the special forces unit sweeping the last three events in four years.
“The 75th Ranger Regiment is a one-of-a-kind unit,” Doyle said, an Army release states. “We simply show up to work every day focused on marksmanship, small unit tactics, medical training and mobility.”
Sgt. Maj. of the Army Michael R. Weimer presented the awards to Shield and Doyle, as well as to the soldiers that rounded out the best squad, which included Sgt. William Masters, Spc. William Schaeffer and Spc. Marshall Garren.
After securing its place in the competition and being named the Army Special Operations Command top squad in August, the five-soldier squad found themselves in the muck and mire of Fort Benning.
During the 2026 competition, events ranged from fitness assessments, weapons qualifications, medical scenarios and an 18.6-mile nighttime foot march and obstacle course. Competitors also experienced the “First 100 Yards” evolution that replaced the traditional “shark attack” opening day for recruits, the release said. The soldiers also completed the combat water survival course, loaded and fired from an M1A2 Abrams and rounded out the competition with interviews with review boards.
“The Army Best Squad Competition is important because it shows where the readiness of the different commands is at across the entire Army,” Shield said. “And on top of that, competition is a huge part of the Army. And who doesn’t want to be first?”
This is the first Best Squad competition in two years after the yearly competition was canceled in 2025 due to a “lapse in appropriations” caused by Congress’ failure to pass a fiscal 2026 budget.
In 2022, Rangers earned the title of Best Squad and swept all three awards the following year. In 2024, a team from the U.S. Army Pacific won Best Squad.
Claire Barrett is an editor and military history correspondent for Military Times. She holds a master's degree in military history from King's College, London, and is also a World War II researcher with an unparalleled affinity for Sir Winston Churchill and Michigan football.

articles.title: US Army to address parents’ blocked access to teen medical records
articles.snippet: Military parents face barriers in getting access to the medical records of their children aged 13 to 18.
articles.full_text:
To military parents who are frustrated because they can’t get access to their teenagers’ medical records, the U.S. Army Surgeon General has a message: “We share your concern,” and are working to address it.
Currently, parents don’t have access to a child’s medical records from the time they turn 13, “based on current departmental policy,” Lt. Gen. Mary K. Izaguirre said Tuesday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.
In addition, children don’t have ID cards to sign in to the Defense Enrollment Eligibility System (DEERS), she said. Children must be at least 18 to log in to the system.
The question of parents’ access came up during a family forum at AUSA. Izaguirre said the issue is one of her husband’s favorite topics, and “I share his passion for it,” she said.
For now, parents must go to the patient administration offices at their military treatment facilities and have their teenage children sign consent forms to give parents permission for access to their medical records.
“That’s a barrier,” Izaguirre said, adding that “we’ve been working with the [Defense Health Agency], and the [Department of Health and Human Services]” to address the hurdle.
The issue stems from privacy laws and has come up in various settings with military families.
Researchers with the organization Feedback were “surprised at how often this came up, not just one parent at one base,” said Erin Domagola, the research director at the organization. Feedback analyzed comments received in the Federal Register, following a Defense Department solicitation in March for comments and suggestions from military families on how DoD could improve their quality of life.
Feedback uses applied anthropology, behavioral science and digital ethnography to understand what people experience and why.
The company independently analyzed Federal Register military family comments from 2024 to 2026 about quality of life. While there were a relatively small number of comments overall —117 in 2026 — it does provide a window into some of the concerns and suggestions, the researchers said.
Karen has covered military families, quality of life and consumer issues for Military Times for more than 30 years, and is co-author of a chapter on media coverage of military families in the book "A Battle Plan for Supporting Military Families." She previously worked for newspapers in Guam, Norfolk, Jacksonville, Fla., and Athens, Ga.

articles.title: Honeywell Aerospace’s counter-drone software unites data from multiple sensors into one
articles.snippet: Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from disparate sources into a single interface.
articles.full_text:
Counter-drone systems can combine radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors and other equipment to detect, track and identify potential threats. Honeywell Aerospace’s SAMURAI system is designed to bring information from those disparate sources into a single interface.
The system uses UNITAS, Honeywell Aerospace’s battle-management software, to integrate sensors and effectors from different manufacturers.
“There is no one solution that solves every threat out there,” said retired Air Force Col. Tom Konicki, director of business at Honeywell Aerospace.
The threat ranges from recreational drones flown into restricted airspace to unmanned aircraft that could be used to attack military installations or other critical infrastructure. Konicki said counter-drone systems need to detect, track, identify, classify and ultimately defeat drones, regardless of the operator’s intent.
“The threat is real, and the threat is now,” he added.
While SAMURAI stands for Stationary and Mobile UAS Reveal and Intercept, UNITAS is not an acronym. Konicki said the name was inspired by football player Johnny Unitas.
Counter-drone systems can combine several types of equipment. Radar detects objects at a distance, while radio-frequency sensors can detect signals associated with drones or their controllers. Remote identification equipment can receive identifying information broadcast by compliant drones. Electro-optical and infrared cameras allow operators to examine objects more closely, while acoustic sensors can help detect drones by their sound.
Depending on the threat and equipment available, counter-drone systems can also use electronic warfare, directed-energy systems, conventional weapons or interceptor drones to defeat an aircraft. Some systems use nets to capture drones, an approach that can be designed to reduce the risk of debris falling onto people or property.
Konicki said operators of some counter-drone systems must monitor six, seven or eight separate screens for radar, cameras, radio-frequency sensors, jamming equipment and other capabilities. That can require one operator to track multiple information streams simultaneously. UNITAS is designed to consolidate the feeds so operators can view information from multiple sensors together in one interface.
“We call it a single pane of glass,” Konicki said. “There could be seven different sensors that have identified it and are feeding that into our software.”
Konicki said the interface is designed to be straightforward for operators, including younger service members who may be assigned counter-drone duties without extensive experience operating the different systems. He said Honeywell Aerospace has demonstrated the software to U.S. government and military representatives, as well as local law enforcement and state and city representatives.
The software also uses an open-architecture approach, allowing customers to integrate equipment they already own instead of replacing it with products from a single manufacturer.
“We’re not asking them to go buy new stuff,” Konicki said. “We can integrate with what they already have.”
Customers can choose equipment suited to their needs and update components as detection technologies and countermeasures evolve. Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with other companies to incorporate their technologies rather than lock customers into a single vendor’s products. He said the company seeks equipment mature enough for operational use rather than untested technology.
At the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting, Honeywell Aerospace displayed a mockup of the mobile configuration mounted on the back of a Ford F-150. Konicki called it the “Green Beast.”
Honeywell Aerospace is also developing an airborne application of SAMURAI with Odys Aviation. Announced in March 2026, the collaboration aims to adapt the system for Odys’ long-range Laila uncrewed aircraft. The companies said the effort builds on more than a year of joint development and systems-integration work. Laila is intended to be the first airborne application of SAMURAI, extending the system beyond ground-based and mobile configurations.
Konicki said SAMURAI can also be configured for fixed-site protection and maritime operations. Depending on the mission, customers might position equipment around a building or installation, use a mobile configuration for temporary protection at an event, or place sensors at distributed locations to cover a larger area.
Separately, Honeywell Aerospace announced Oct. 12 that its wholly owned subsidiary, EMS Defense Technologies, was selected for a Department of Homeland Security counter-drone contract vehicle. The five-year, multiple-award vehicle has a $1.5 billion ceiling, was awarded July 31 and took effect Aug. 1.
Konicki said Honeywell Aerospace works with international partners, including Lithuania, Slovakia and Colombia, and can integrate locally sourced equipment when customers want to use particular sensors or effectors.
For customers protecting an air base or another site, Konicki said the company can assess where radar, cameras and other sensors should be positioned to maximize coverage.
Its planning process can map areas with adequate coverage, identify gaps and recommend adjustments to equipment placement. The company can then conduct what Konicki described as a red-team assessment, examining where an adversary might launch a drone and how that approach could affect the site’s defenses. The analysis will help customers tailor sensor placement and other system components to the site and its potential threats.
Natalie Oliverio is an independent journalist and Navy veteran who covers military and veterans’ issues. Drawing on her experience as a talent executive and mentor, she writes about the policies, people and programs shaping the military community.

articles.title: Acting US Army secretary creates task force for HVAC repairs
articles.snippet: A new, enterprise-level Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning Task Force has identified more than $100 million in projects for early 2027.
articles.full_text:
HVAC problems, particularly air conditioning breakdowns, are not uncommon for U.S. soldiers residing in barracks.
This summer, mechanical problems with a water treatment plant in Hawaii left thousands of soldiers at multiple Army installations on Oahu without central air conditioning. Soldiers at Fort Hood, Texas, experienced five to six weeks of unbearably hot temperatures in their rooms last year before AC was restored.
And just last month, soldiers assigned to Fort Carson, Colorado, reported sleeping in their cars to escape hot barracks rooms, Stars and Stripes reported.
Now, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle is attempting to do something about it. Telle announced Monday at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting the creation of an enterprise-level Heating, Ventilation and Air Conditioning Task Force focused on soldiers’ quality of life.
The task force includes leaders from facility operations, contracting and military engineering who can “cut through bureaucratic silos,” the Army said in a Monday statement.
The announcement follows a directive from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last year to create another military-wide task force to improve barracks.
“Secretary of War Hegseth has said every service member deserves clean, comfortable, and safe housing,” Telle said at the annual meeting in Washington, D.C. “This has never been done before — we’re taking this for the first time to the national level, to deliver results across the country to soldiers.”
Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a statement that HVAC is the top quality-of-life complaint that leadership hears from soldiers.
The Government Accountability Office reported in August that the Defense Department does not request enough funding to fully meet its installation maintenance and major improvement needs, leading to a backlog of deferred maintenance at barracks. Hundreds of thousands of service members live in military barracks, with concerns about poor living conditions and management going back decades, according to the government watchdog.
Before the end of the fiscal year in September, the Army directed $15 million toward 44 high-priority HVAC projects across multiple installations, the service said in a statement.
“While that effort brought immediate relief to specific facilities, the [task force] leaders recognized that one-time emergency funding cannot replace a comprehensive, proactive strategy,” the Army said.
Members of the task force will work directly with garrison commanders to find HVAC projects for 2027 and 2028, the Army said. So far, it has identified more than $100 million in projects to be awarded in early 2027.
“This ensures ready-to-award projects are pre-engineered and priced as soon as funds become available,” the service said. “Additionally, the [task force] will utilize regional contracting approaches, utility energy service contracts, and commercial best practices.”
Nikki Wentling is a senior editor at Military Times. She's reported on veterans and military communities for over a decade and has also covered technology, politics, health care and crime. Her work has earned multiple honors from the National Coalition for Homeless Veterans, the Arkansas Associated Press Managing Editors and others.

articles.title: US soldiers must train on ‘new basics’ of unmanned systems, officials say
articles.snippet: As the U.S. Army trains soldiers for multi-domain operations, the service needs to prepare them with “new basics."
articles.full_text:
As the U.S. Army trains soldiers for multi-domain operations, like in the multinational exercise Project Flytrap, the service needs to prepare them with “new basics” to establish one standard and baseline, officials said.
Within the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, or 2CR, new basics include unmanned aerial systems operation and employment, counter-UAS systems and unmanned ground vehicle usage, service officials said during a Monday discussion at the Association of the U.S. Army annual meeting, titled “Project Flytrap—Accelerating Offensive Maneuver through Data-Centric Kill Web.”
Project Flytrap is an Army counter-unmanned aerial systems initiative and multinational exercise, which has leveled up from the individual soldier to the squadron level with multiple iterations.
The most recent exercise, Project Flytrap 5.0, took place in Lithuania and was concluded earlier this year with partner nations, including the United Kingdom and Australia, and was led by the Army’s V Corps. The countries integrated and tested more than 50 industry-provided technologies, launched effects and unmanned ground vehicles and tested against a live opposing force.
“The American way of war is centered on maneuver, and counter-UAS cannot remain tied to static defense,” Col. Timothy Price, commander of the 2nd Cavalry Regiment, said in a Tuesday release. “Project FlyTrap ensures we maintain mobility and offensive survivability in a highly contested, opaque operational environment.”
The 2nd Cavalry Regiment is expanding Project Flytrap into a battalion-level operational capability, adapting from small-unit field trials into tactical employment connected with operational objectives aimed at breaking through drone-saturated frontlines on Europe’s Eastern Flank.
“As we’re training our soldiers for the multi-domain operations, or multi-domain breeds, we talk about the new basics inside of 2CR,” Command Sgt. Maj. Jesse Clark, 2nd Cavalry Regiment senior enlisted leader, said during Monday’s discussion.
“With the new basics, we need to focus on sUAS, counter-UAS, camouflage for electromagnetic signatures … and how we’re going to do that so soldiers understand how to camouflage themselves with those spectrum options,” he continued.
Officials listed the previous basics to include topics such as marksmanship, map reading and navigation, radio etiquette and UAS and jamming reaction to contact.
Clark said the service needs to have disciplined unit training management in which personnel, time and equipment are included to ensure soldiers are proficient at the new basics. One way to complete this is to have a series of expert badges.
“Everyone needs to know these basics because it’s going to be required whether you’re on the frontline or you’re back in the rear because we’re going to have UAS all over the place,” Clark said.
The U.S. military has strived to incorporate UAS and counter-UAS training across all branches, with new units in the Marine Corps and the Defense Innovation Unit aiming to recruit service members with first-person-view drone experience to participate in the Pentagon’s Drone Dominance program.
Cristina Stassis is a reporter covering stories surrounding the defense industry, national security, military/veteran affairs and more. She previously worked as an editorial fellow for Defense News in 2024 where she assisted the newsroom in breaking news across Sightline Media Group.

articles.title: NORTHCOM’s Joint Task Force-Gold to coordinate cyber warfare for Golden Dome
articles.snippet: Col. Kevin “Stoney” Stonerook, deputy commander of US Northern Command’s Joint Task Force-Gold (JTF-Gold), said the unit’s roles and responsibilities are still being ironed out.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — US Northern Command’s (NORTHCOM) task force for coordinating Golden Dome homeland air and missile defense capabilities across the Joint Force has been newly charged with enabling related cyberwar capabilities, according to a senior official.
Col. Kevin “Stoney” Stonerook, deputy commander of Joint Task Force-Gold (JTF-Gold), told reporters here today at the annual Association of the US Army conference that cyber warfare “has become a new mission set for us.”
“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholder communities — be that vendors and other government agencies — to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA, and that’s one of the main things that we’re really focused on,” he said.
In later comments to Breaking Defense, however, Stonerook stressed that task force’s cyber activities were focused only on defense against adversary attacks on Golden Dome capabilities, rather than offensive activities.
NORTHCOM announced JTF-Gold with little fanfare, and almost no information, in January. The announcement noted that the head of Army Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC) — a position held since April by Lt. Gen. John Rafferty — would be double-hatted as leader of the the task force, and co-located with SMDC at Peterson SFB, Colo.
“This new command enhances the integration and synchronization of the homeland’s integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) enterprise,” the announcement said.
Stonerook explained that JTF-Gold was created “out of the ashes” of US Space Command’s former Joint Force Component Command for Integrated Missile Defense. That component command’s mission “was really to take all things … of the missile defense system and make sure that that was well coordinated and orchestrated across the joint force,” he said.
“JTF-Gold was stood up to operationalize Golden Dome for America (GDA) for USNORTHCOM,” Stonerook said, and now sports about 100 personnel.
One of the the task force’s first missions has been to help develop “some of the sites as we look at building out GDA across the country and other areas, and trying to integrate all those capabilities across the multiple layers of GDA,” he said.
Stonerook said JTF-Gold was involved in siting and construction activities for Golden Dome’s first operational site at Fort Story, Va., and will do the same at all future sites.
“But there’s a lot we still have to figure out,” he acknowledged.
For example, Stonerook said, Space Command’s integrated missile defense component command managed “all the assets across the missile defense system.” But now that JTF-Gold is under NORTHCOM, there is a need to figure out how to split those responsibilities.
“So, we’re still waiting to see where everything is falling out and whether those is needed redundancies. But our team is responsible for asset management, but the clear delineation of which assets are included and not included has not been completed.”
To that end, Stonerook said, JTF-Gold held a large “planning sprint” in February.
“We had over 300 people join us in Colorado Springs as we got a team of teams together to really understand who was doing what across the entirety of the GDA stakeholder community, and it was really beneficial,” he said. “It really kick started some of the planning, and we were able to develop concept of operations and continue on with a lot of the planning with things that were questions that were unanswered.”
Stonerook said that the next such planning sprint will be at the end of the month, focused on figuring out the respective responsibilities of the three “major” operations centers for Golden Dome at Peterson, Schriever SFB, Colo., and Tyndall AFB, Fla.
“What those roles and responsibilities are and where those lines are drawn, where there’s necessary redundancy, is still an active discussion. So, the planning sprint that we have at the end of the month, that’s one of the main topics of things that we’re going to get after,” he said. “[W]ho should be doing what, are we resourced to do those things, and what additional capabilities are there?”

articles.title: UK Legal Aid Agency hack worse than thought, with stolen records dating back to 1978
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A cyberattack on Britain’s Legal Aid Agency (LAA) stole far older and broader records than the government previously disclosed.
articles.full_text:
UK Legal Aid Agency hack worse than thought, with stolen records dating back to 1978
A cyberattack on Britain’s Legal Aid Agency (LAA) stole far older and broader records than the government previously disclosed, officials said Wednesday.
While initially claimed to have affected people who had used the service since 2010, the breach is now believed to include about 250,000 records predating 2007 and to include data on additional people who were being supervised by the probation service.
Justice Minister Sarah Sackman described the incident as “significant and complex” in a written statement to Parliament.
She explained the cyberattack “happened because criminals were able to exploit vulnerabilities in the LAA’s IT systems and gain access to systems containing personal information. They then copied and exfiltrated some data held by the department.”
The agency disclosed last May that hackers accessed data from people who applied for legal aid through its online service since 2010, potentially compromising data including criminal histories.
At the time, charities warned the data — believed to have been stolen by cyber extortionists — could contain sensitive information about women and girls who survived domestic abuse situations.
In an update published Wednesday, the Legal Aid Agency said continuing forensic analysis found more data was accessed than initially believed.
“The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and May 16, 2025, or to cases that were live during this period,” it said.
“However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007. The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978.”
According to the forensic analysis, the stolen material also includes probation data covering names, dates of birth, nationalities and case reference numbers.
“It is important to put this updated information in context,” said the agency. “The presence of records predating 2007 does not mean that everyone who received or applied for legal aid, or otherwise interacted with the justice system before 2007, has been affected.”
It said the information exfiltrated varies between individual cases but can include full names, dates of birth, National Insurance numbers, ZIP codes, equality monitoring codes, case start and end dates, costs claimed, the amount of VAT claimed or paid as well as codes indicating the type of legal aid received.
Other categories include financial assessments of defendants and their partners, details of bank accounts and property, and in some cases partially redacted payment card details.
The names of judges, defense and prosecution lawyers, and court reporters involved in Crown Court trials over the same periods were also taken. So were details of opposing parties in some civil cases, according to the update.
The agency said the breach was hard to assess because much of the stolen data was “unstructured, fragmented, or incomplete.” It added that earlier public statements reflected the best information available at the time.
Sackman told the House of Commons that the department has no indication the stolen data has been published or shared — a shift in view from May 2025, when a ministry spokesperson told Recorded Future News that its publication was a question of “when, not if.”
The hackers had claimed to hold data on more than 2 million people and threatened to release it unless they received payment. The British government has a longstanding policy of refusing to pay extortion demands.
Sackman said the ministry has since strengthened authentication and access controls, improved security monitoring and begun retiring or isolating higher-risk legacy systems. It continues to work with the National Crime Agency, the National Cyber Security Centre and the Information Commissioner's Office, the U.K.’s data protection regulator.

articles.title: UK Legal Aid Agency: Hackers stole records dating back to 1978
articles.snippet: The Legal Aid Agency (LAA), an executive agency of the UK's Ministry of Justice that manages the country's Public Defender Service, says attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating back to 1978. [...]
articles.full_text:
The Legal Aid Agency (LAA), an executive agency of the UK's Ministry of Justice that manages the country's Public Defender Service, says attackers who breached its IT systems in April 2025 stole records dating back to 1978.
The agency employs around 1,250 staff, oversees billions in legal funding, and works with approximately 2,000 providers, including barristers, solicitor firms, and non-profit organizations that deliver civil and criminal legal aid services in England and Wales.
The LAA disclosed the cyberattack in early May 2025, warning that payment information for legal aid providers might have been compromised.
Two weeks later, it confirmed the resulting data breach was more serious than first believed after finding that attackers had stolen a large trove of sensitive applicant and recipient data from 2010 onward, including contact details, dates of birth, national ID numbers, criminal history, employment status, as well as contribution amounts, debts, and payments.
The threat actors have also stolen legal aid providers' data, including provider contracts, office locations, financial information, contact details, LAA Online Portal credentials (including names and email addresses), and more.
In an update published this week, the LAA said follow-up analysis of the exfiltrated data found that the stolen records go back almost five decades.
"The vast majority of the LAA data relates to applications, claims or payments submitted to the LAA between January 2007 and 16 May 2025, or to cases that were live during this period. However, we have now confirmed that approximately 250,000 records predate 2007," the agency said. "The overwhelming majority of these are from the 1990s and 2000s, with only a fractionally small number dating from before 1990. The earliest record currently verified dates from 1978."
However, it noted that records predating 2007 do not mean everyone who received, applied for legal aid, or interacted with the justice system before 2007 was affected.
"We recognise that incidents of this nature are concerning for anyone affected. That is why we published information on GOV. UK as quickly as possible and have continued to update it as our understanding of the cyber-attack has developed," a Ministry of Justice spokesperson told BleepingComputer.
"Prior to the cyber-attack, we had already committed £20 million to stabilising and upgrading the Legal Aid Agency's digital systems. We are now investing more than £200 million in modernising digital services, improving resilience and strengthening cyber security across legal aid services. There is currently no evidence that any personal data believed to have been exfiltrated has been published."
After the LAA breach, which was followed by a string of cyberattacks targeting the Co-op, Harrods, and Marks & Spencer (M&S) UK retail chains claimed by the DragonForce ransomware operation, the country's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) published guidance and advised UK organizations to follow it to strengthen their cybersecurity defenses.
In January, the UK also announced a new cybersecurity strategy, backed by more than £210 million ($283 million), to boost cyber defenses across government departments and the wider public sector.
This week, the UK Housing Ombudsman Service, a non-departmental public body sponsored by the Ministry of Housing that settles disputes between social housing residents and social landlords in England, disclosed that it is investigating a third-party IT security incident that impacted its case management system.

articles.title: Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers target governments across former Soviet states
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A roughly 2-year-old cyber-espionage campaign against Central Asian states appears to originate in Kazakhstan, researchers said.
articles.full_text:
Suspected Kazakhstan-linked hackers target governments across former Soviet states
A cyber-espionage group with suspected ties to Kazakhstan has targeted government agencies across Central Asia and other former Soviet states, seeking information on diplomatic affairs, economic policy and strategic resources, according to new research.
The hackers, tracked as UAT-6275 by Cisco Talos and TAG-193 by Recorded Future's Insikt Group, have conducted at least eight campaigns since January 2025, the two teams said in jointly issued reports. The Record is an editorially independent unit of Recorded Future.
The campaign targeted or showed interest in government institutions across nine countries, including Russia, Belarus, Armenia, Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, the researchers said.
Researchers said the hackers appeared particularly interested in government agencies responsible for foreign affairs, economic development, agriculture and environmental management, as well as information about regional energy supplies and water resources.
“These organizations hold information that can inform negotiations, economic planning, and regional security decisions,” the Insikt Group said. “Across Central Asia, shared river systems and interconnected energy and transport infrastructure give such information particular strategic value.”
Local clues
Researchers assessed with medium confidence that the hacking group has ties to Kazakhstan.
The clues include Russian-language material found in the malware, evidence suggesting that malicious software was tested from Kazakhstan shortly after it was created, and hacking activity that generally matched working hours in the country's time zone.
The group's operations also overlap with earlier cyber-espionage campaigns linked to YoroTrooper, a suspected Kazakhstan-based threat actor that emerged in 2022 and has primarily targeted governments in Central Asia and neighboring countries.
In one of its latest attacks, TAG-193 hackers targeted a Tajik government entity shortly after treaty discussions with Kazakhstan in March 2026. Another operation targeted a Belarusian government entity ahead of a bilateral meeting in April.
Researchers said the timing could indicate an interest in diplomatic developments, although it does not establish what information the hackers were seeking or whether they obtained it.
The group also showed interest in environmental and natural resource management, including an Armenian government agency responsible for environmental affairs and Uzbekistan's Smart Forestry initiative.
Hacking techniques
The group typically attempts to compromise its targets through phishing emails containing malicious attachments, sometimes sent from legitimate government email accounts that have already been compromised.
The emails use official-looking documents, including diplomatic correspondence, aviation forms and business proposals.
Researchers said the hackers also used GitHub, the software development platform, to store malicious scripts and files, helping their operations blend in with legitimate online activity.
In April 2026, the group was observed exploiting a security vulnerability in the file compression program WinRAR in an operation likely targeting Armenia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The flaw, tracked as CVE-2025-8088, allowed the attackers to place malware in a Windows folder that automatically runs programs when a user signs in.
Researchers said it was the first time they had observed the group exploiting a software vulnerability to deliver malware, suggesting it was expanding its methods beyond deceptive emails and documents.
Researchers expect the group to continue targeting diplomatic institutions and government agencies responsible for managing strategic resources across the region.
“Its sustained operations and adoption of additional delivery techniques suggest continued investment in gaining access to institutions holding information of strategic interest,” they added.

articles.title: Ukraine says Elon Musk's Starshield service partially restored after restrictions disrupted drone missions
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The Ukrainian military can again use SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service on the move, a Defense Ministry source told Recorded Future News on Thursday, days after sudden restrictions disrupted drone missions along the front line.
articles.full_text:
Ukraine says Elon Musk's Starshield service partially restored after restrictions disrupted drone missions
The Ukrainian military can again use SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service on the move, a Defense Ministry source told Recorded Future News on Thursday, days after sudden restrictions disrupted drone missions along the front line.
Starshield, a military-grade version of SpaceX’s Starlink internet service, keeps Ukrainian units connected through terminals mounted on vehicles and drones as they travel.
Overnight Tuesday, without warning, that connection was disrupted as new restrictions limited how fast a terminal could move and still hold a connection — forcing troops to cancel combat missions and complicating drone operations, logistics and reconnaissance.
“Starshield connectivity while in motion has now been restored and remains operational,” the source said, citing reports from military units and speaking anonymously because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The ministry told Recorded Future News on Wednesday that connections had improved at speeds of up to 160 kilometers per hour (about 100 mph), though the formal speed limit remained in place.
The cause of the restrictions remains unclear. Officials are in talks with SpaceX and its partners to find out, the source said.
Musk points to Washington
Responding Wednesday to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who called for the speed limits to be lifted entirely, Musk said the U.S. government controlled Starshield and was responsible for deciding how the service could be used.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government. Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," Musk wrote on X.
Fedorov said removing Starshield’s speed limit was critical for Ukraine's defense and expressed hope that Musk would continue supporting the country.
Musk, however, drew a distinction between Starshield and SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, saying the latter was intended for civilian or defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations.
The comments appeared to shift responsibility for the restrictions toward Washington, although officials in President Donald Trump's administration have reportedly denied involvement.
Administration officials told Axios that the U.S. government did not control SpaceX and had not ordered the restrictions. Washington nevertheless planned to contact the company to determine what caused the disruptions.
Drone missions disrupted
The restrictions have already had consequences on the battlefield, particularly for Ukrainian drones that depend on satellite connectivity for navigation and control.
Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said units operating in the Huliaipole sector in southern Ukraine began reporting communication problems overnight Tuesday as the new limits took effect.
According to the military, some drones experienced connection losses lasting between 10 and 20 seconds while traveling at speeds of just 110 to 120 kilometers per hour — well below the formally established threshold.
Although the drones continued flying, the interruptions made them harder to control. Slowing them down to maintain connectivity also increased their vulnerability to Russian attacks.
The problem was particularly severe for medium-range strike drones, which require relatively high speeds during takeoff.
Under the new conditions, unstable communications could make it impossible to launch some drones or use them for their intended missions, the military said.
At least one drone unit operating in the Huliaipole sector was forced to cancel some missions because of connectivity problems.
Serhii Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military technology expert and presidential adviser, said the restrictions also threatened Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian drones.
He said Starlink was essential to interceptor drones used against high-speed, jet-powered Shahed drones, warning that the restrictions could deprive Ukraine of one of its few effective defenses against those weapons.
“Our defense forces received no advance warning of the restriction, which caused several missions to fail. Clearly, this move cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” he added but didn’t provide further details.
Zelensky blames Trump
The Starlink disruption comes amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington, following disputes over Ukrainian strikes against Russian oil infrastructure and the Trump administration's decision to pursue a diesel trade agreement with Moscow.
In an interview with Piers Morgan this week, Zelensky said he felt personally betrayed by Trump over the restrictions, accusing Washington of abandoning a crucial partner more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.
The Ukrainian president alleged that both SpaceX and the United States were responsible for the disruption, which he said would cost Ukrainian lives.
"I am sure they knew what they did, absolutely," Zelensky said, adding that the restrictions would result in further casualties.
The Kremlin, meanwhile, said it had no official information confirming the reported restrictions. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov added that Moscow would prefer technologies such as Starlink not to be used for military purposes in the war.
A critical technology for Ukraine
Starlink has played a central role in Ukraine's military communications since the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, when Musk activated the service following an appeal from Fedorov.
SpaceX subsequently provided thousands of terminals, helping Ukraine restore communications damaged by Russian attacks.
But Musk's relationship with Kyiv has become increasingly complicated. He has previously raised concerns about the costs of providing the service and the risks of its use in offensive military operations. In a separate statement yesterday, he even suggested that “it’s time for Zelensky to go.”
In March 2025, however, Musk pledged never to disconnect Ukraine from Starlink, acknowledging the Ukrainian military's dependence on the technology.
Earlier this year, SpaceX also took steps to prevent unauthorized Russian use of Starlink after Ukrainian officials reported that Russian forces were installing the terminals on attack drones. Ukraine also introduced a verification system that allows only registered Starlink devices to operate in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Suspected sabotage
The latest restrictions come as Starlink-related infrastructure supporting Ukraine has also faced suspected sabotage in Europe.
In September, a fire damaged electrical equipment at a Starlink ground station in Poland. Polish authorities investigated possible sabotage, with prosecutors saying they had grounds to suspect the perpetrators could have acted on behalf of Russian intelligence services.
Earlier this week, two masked men deliberately set fire to 11 of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Bulgaria's capital, Sofia, according to local authorities. The antennas were used by Ukraine and other customers.
There is no publicly confirmed evidence linking the two incidents or establishing Russian involvement in the Bulgarian attack.

articles.title: North Macedonian police arrest alleged administrator behind OLVX cybercrime market
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: A raid on a home in a North Macedonian village led to the arrest of the suspected administrator of the OLVX market, according to the Balkan country's Interior Ministry along with the FBI.
articles.full_text:
North Macedonian police arrest alleged administrator behind OLVX cybercrime market
The administrator behind a cybercriminal marketplace called OLVX was arrested this week in North Macedonia in a joint operation between the Balkan country’s Ministry of Interior and the FBI.
The suspect was not named, but the FBI and North Macedonia said a raid on the man’s home in the village of Golema Rečica was conducted after charges were filed.
Since 2023, OLVX has become a popular market where cybercriminals share stolen personal data, login credentials and other tools to help with cybercrime.
“Active between 2023 and 2025, OLVX is alleged to have unlawfully sold victims’ personally identifiable information and login credentials via over 1,500 seller accounts,” the FBI said in a statement. “The existence of this marketplace directly endangered the digital security of thousands of American citizens who rely on the integrity of accounts they use.”
North Macedonian police said the suspect also ran another group called ONEMILI on Telegram that offered tools for fraudulent refund schemes and other scams.
“Additionally, evidence was obtained indicating that the suspect had acquired and possessed child sexual abuse material (CSAM) for personal use through the Telegram application,” North Macedonia’s Interior Ministry said.
Cybersecurity firm ZeroFox published a lengthy investigation into OLVX in 2023, warning that the site was becoming increasingly popular among cybercriminals selling phishing kits, remote desktop connections, credentials, stolen data and other tools.
The site allowed criminals to pay each other through cryptocurrency instead of operating an escrow service like many other underground marketplaces. Users loaded funds onto the site and paid each other with the funds sent to the platform.
Law enforcement agencies have taken down dozens of cybercriminal marketplaces over the last five years as the sites have become focal points for hackers exchanging stolen data, tools and tactics.
Last week, the co-creator of a dark web cybercriminal forum called Empire Market was sentenced to 40 years in federal prison.
Microsoft announced its own takedown on Wednesday of three popular Chinese phishing sites used by Chinese cybercriminals to send hundreds of millions of malicious messages impersonating over 75,000 organizations worldwide.

articles.title: Brooklyn DA’s office disrupts crypto scam targeting Russian community
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Russian-speaking Brooklyn residents began tipping off local authorities to a cryptocurrency fraud scheme three years ago, leading to an operation to take down the associated servers and domains.
articles.full_text:
Brooklyn DA’s office disrupts crypto scam targeting Russian community
Hundreds of web domains and servers were taken down by law enforcement agencies in New York City as part of an operation to stop a cryptocurrency fraud scheme targeting the Russian community in Brooklyn.
Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said his office worked with the FBI to seize and disrupt 241 web domains and 112 servers after the tools were used to steal millions.
The investigation began three years ago when a large number of Russian-speaking victims in Brooklyn told prosecutors they responded to Facebook ads in Russian offering investment opportunities. An investment adviser called them and walked them through the process of creating cryptocurrency accounts and transferring funds on investment platforms.
When the victims tried to take their money out, they were locked out of their accounts and told they had to pay additional fees and taxes in order to get their funds.
Gonzalez’s office said victims likely lost millions but authorities were able to claw back about $300,000 worth of stolen funds.
Several of the seized websites were made to look like legitimate investment platforms and referenced U.S. government agencies or wealthy people like Elon Musk.
Investigators found that criminals used IP addresses and infrastructure in Ukraine and several other Eastern European countries. Search warrants were executed in several countries allowing law enforcement to seize domains and servers.
The servers contained victim information, data for the websites and operational software. The seized data also showed that the scammers were running a secondary operation where they would contact victims weeks after the initial scam and offer to recover their stolen cryptocurrency for a price.
“These criminals stole many millions of dollars from Russian-speaking victims through an elaborate investment scheme, then tried to exploit them again with false promises to recover their money,” Gonzalez said.
Gonzalez noted that his office has taken several similar actions over the last two years, disrupting and seizing about 400 domains associated with cryptocurrency investment fraud.
Despite such efforts, new scam websites continued to re-emerge quickly — prompting law enforcement to specifically target the European backend servers powering the sites.
Cryptocurrency investment fraud continues to be one of the most costly scams plaguing U.S. residents.
A Treasury Department report released last month said between September 2023 and December 2025, more than $12.7 billion was stolen from Americans in cryptocurrency investment scams from victims in all 50 states and U.S. territories.

articles.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
articles.snippet: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.
On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.
As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.
The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.
“Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”
In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.
TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.
Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.
“A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”
As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said.
Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.
Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.
Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.
That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.
“Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.”

articles.title: Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws
articles.snippet: Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today's epic patch batch dwarfs September's record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.
Just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.
Windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).
At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.
While Microsoft said there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.
Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.
“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he said.
Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.
Tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.
“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.
Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.
One has to wonder how big the backlog of flaws is at this point. Maybe this month’s increase in the number of fixes just reflects an increasing number of people working on these fixes, and that they already have enough flaws to keep them all busy for a long time. Oh to be a fly on the wall.
